one_liner: Rust multi-transport web framework on hyper; its thread-per-core HTTP/1.1 server out-served Drogon 1.12-1.24x in the-benchmarker.
what_it_does: Tako is an Axum-style Rust framework (routers, typed extractors, middleware plugins, OpenAPI, GraphQL, gRPC, WebSocket, SSE, raw TCP/UDP) that serves HTTP/1.1, h2, h3 and WebTransport on Tokio or Compio. The catalogued fast path is the optional `per-thread` feature: `serve_per_thread(addr, router, PerThreadConfig::default())` starts one OS thread per available CPU, each with its own current-thread runtime and SO_REUSEPORT listener, sharing one Arc<Router>. It is a framework you write handlers against, not a drop-in replacement for a C++ server binary.
how_it_is_fast: The HTTP/1.1 engine is hyper's http1 connection driver (keep-alive, pipeline_flush on, TCP_NODELAY set per socket); tako's contribution is the thread-per-core shell: current-thread Tokio runtimes driving connections with spawn_local so requests never cross threads, kernel SO_REUSEPORT fan-out, and a least-live-connections hand-off (balance_connections, on by default) that moves a freshly accepted socket to a less busy worker over an unbounded channel. The 2.4 docs add that a hello-world request no longer allocates. Actix Web and ntex use the same shape, and the author's own wrk runs put per-thread 3-17% ahead of Actix Web and 27-31% ahead of tako's default multi-thread server (3.2x at 100 loopback connections).
when_to_use: Linux HTTP/1.1 APIs in Rust that want a full framework (extractors, middleware, OpenAPI, gRPC) with hyper-class throughput: in the-benchmarker tako matched plain hyper within 2% and beat Drogon 1.9.13 by 1.12-1.24x.
Keep-alive or pipelined HTTP/1.1 traffic at high connection counts: HttpArena pipelined-4096 22.1M req/s vs plain hyper 16.2M and Drogon 7.8M; baseline-4096 3.26M vs hyper 3.00M and actix 2.78M.

CPU-constrained deployments where cost per request matters: derived from the-benchmarker's core counts, tako used about 10.2 us of server CPU per request at 64 connections versus Drogon's 14.3 us, and HttpArena latency-1m held the same 1M req/s target at 2,641% CPU versus Drogon's 3,552%.
One codebase that must also expose WebSocket, gRPC, SSE or raw TCP/UDP listeners next to the HTTP API under a single router and middleware model.
when_not_to_use: HTTP/2, h2c or HTTP/3 heavy services: per-thread workers serve HTTP/1.1 only, and tako's multi-thread h2 path served 741,740 req/s on HttpArena baseline-h2-256 versus 6,974,787 for the plain hyper entry and 3,884,214 for actix (h2c-256: 747,323 vs actix 5,918,827).
Thousands of concurrent WebSocket connections: echo-ws-4096 420,836 msg/s versus actix 3,409,380 (tied at 512 connections), and echo-ws-pipeline-4096 5.35M versus actix 43.1M.
Compressed JSON with the stock compression plugin: json-comp-4096 212,739 req/s versus actix 541,211.

Teams that need a stable, widely used framework: one maintainer, 5,191 crates.io downloads, Rust 1.95+ with edition 2024, and five releases from 2.1.0 (2026-09-27) to 2.4.1 (2026-10-11), with migration guides for 2.1, 2.2, 2.3 and 2.4.

Expecting a win over the fastest C servers: HttpArena puts it level with nginx on baseline-4096 (3,258,564 vs 3,284,513) and far behind on static TLS and HTTP/2; Nim PowPow and Dart jet_server rows outscore it in the-benchmarker.

integration.form: crate (tako-rs on crates.io, imported as `tako`; `per-thread` feature pulls in tako-rs-server-pt)
integration.dependencies: tokio, hyper 1.x, hyper-util, socket2 (per-thread server); optional compio, rustls, quinn/h3, core_affinity, tikv-jemallocator, tonic and many integrations behind cargo features
integration.platforms: Linux for the per-thread server's kernel load balancing (SO_REUSEPORT); on macOS/BSD and Windows the Tokio workers rely on the balance_connections hand-off and the code warns when it is off; Compio flavour targets io_uring, IOCP or kqueue
integration.thread_safety: Router is shared across worker threads through an Arc; each connection and its handler futures stay on one worker's current-thread runtime (spawn_local); cross-request shared state must be thread-safe

gotchas: The same table that shows the Drogon win also shows it is hyper's: the-benchmarker's plain hyper 1.5 entry (about 40 lines, default multi-thread work-stealing Tokio runtime, one listener) scored 216,185 / 201,964 / 198,218 req/s at 64 / 256 / 512 connections, within 2% of tako's 219,732 / 200,361 / 193,822, and actix 4.8 and khttp sit in the same band, all at 55-62% server CPU saturation. In this generator-bound run the thread-per-core design adds nothing measurable over plain hyper; it does show up in HttpArena (baseline-4096 1.08x, pipelined-4096 1.36x over hyper).

Likely baseline handicap: the-benchmarker's Drogon config sets threads_num 0, which Drogon 1.9.13 (ConfigLoader.cc) resolves with std::thread::hardware_concurrency(). glibc-based implementations ignore CPU affinity there, so inside a --cpuset-cpus container sized to 4 cores on a 16-CPU host Drogon probably started about 16 event loops, while tako's available_parallelism() honours the cpuset (inferred, not observed). Drogon's latency profile fits that oversubscription: p50 0.1-0.7 ms but p99 11-21 ms, against tako's p99 0.3-2.7 ms, roughly equal to its p50.

HttpArena rows mix servers: per its meta.json only plain HTTP/1.1 and WebSocket on :8080 use the per-thread server; json-tls (904,303 vs Drogon 253,055), h2, h2c and h3 run tako's multi-thread Server. The tako entry there is built with -C target-cpu=native and fat LTO against a generic Drogon build, uses tako 2.4.1 (the-benchmarker snapshot predates 2.4.1, so it ran 2.4.0), and is maintained by tako's author.

Per-thread defaults changed recently: pin_to_core went off by default in 2.4.0 (the author measured pinning 3% slower on loopback and 5% faster pipelined), balance_connections is on, and header_read_timeout closes idle connections after 30-45 s. TLS, h2c and PROXY-protocol listeners need the regular Server builder, so a mixed deployment runs two runtimes in one process, as the HttpArena entry does.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick tako over actix-web or ntex when HTTP/1.1 throughput and a multi-transport router in one crate matter most: it edged actix 4.8 by 1.03-1.05x in the-benchmarker and 1.17x on HttpArena baseline-4096, and its own wrk runs put it 3-17% ahead of Actix Web. Choose actix-web for h2, many WebSocket connections or compressed JSON, where actix leads by 2.5-8x on HttpArena, and note that jet_server and PowPow posted higher the-benchmarker rates than tako.
verified_claims_summary: the-benchmarker data.json (updated 2026-10-06; zrk closed-loop keep-alive on GET /, GET /user/:id and POST /user, server pinned to 4 of 16 cores on an x86_64 host whose CPU string 'M1 Eight-Core Processor' is unidentifiable): tako 2.4 per-thread 219,732 / 200,361 / 193,822 req/s versus Drogon 1.9.13 (GCC from Debian trixie, CMake release, no LTO) 177,005 / 178,341 / 171,358 at 64 / 256 / 512 connections, 1.12-1.24x, with both servers at 56-63% CPU saturation. HttpArena on a Threadripper PRO 3995WX confirms the HTTP/1.1 lead over Drogon (baseline-4096 1.61x, pipelined-4096 2.83x) with a native-tuned tako build.
status_note: Actively developed by a single maintainer (all recent commits by dancixx, 2.4.1 released 2026-10-11), MIT, 163 stars and about 5,200 crates.io downloads; usable for HTTP/1.1-heavy Linux services, but young and churning fast, so pin the minor version.
